newsitem.title: CHINA: IPO VIEW - China telecom, aviation IPOs to be HK focus.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW - China telecom, aviation IPOs to be HK focus.

text.p: Initial public offerings (IPOs) by China-backed airline and telecommunications groups are likely to grab the market focus in Hong Kong in the second half of 1997, analysts say.
Analysts said the two industries were expected to be the centre of market gossip because of their potentially big issue sizes and their concept of tapping growth in the China market.
Of the two industries, telecommunications is expected to generate more excitement in view of its relatively stronger growth potential in the enormous China market, analysts said.
"It provides foreign investors a channel to tap the China telecom market, one which has a population of over one billion," said Sunny Chan, research manager from Seapower Securities.

China Telecom (Hong Kong), a telecommuncations operator controlled by China's Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications, is expected to raise about US$6 billion through a listing in Hong Kong by the end of 1997, market sources said.
Last month, China Telecom agreed to buy a 5.5 percent stake in Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd from Cable and Wireless Plc for HK$14.25 a share.
Analysts said it was still too early to say how good the fundamentals of the China Telecom issue would be, although it was seen to be the biggest IPO in the next six months in Hong Kong.

"It will depend on the composition of its assets and the use of (listing) proceeds. The issue will be unexciting if it uses the proceeds to fund purchase of the Hongkong Telecom stake," said Lawrence Ang, head of China research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

China Aerospace International Holdings Ltd, an arm of the state-owned China Aerospace Corp, has also said it will spin off telecommunications equipment maker and global positioning systems operater, CASIL Telecom, later this year.
IPOs by telecom companies without strong China links are also expected, but are likely to generate less exitement.
"IPOs of those (China concept) telecoms are welcomed as we see promising growth in China, compared with other Asian markets," said Pamela Lam, analyst at Pacific Challenge.
Analysts said airlines, the other expected focus of the IPO market, were a riskier business compared to the telecommunications industry.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said in a June research report that China's aviation sector was facing challenges, including low consumer affordability, a highly competitive and fragmented market structure, and high leverage.
Guangzhou-based China Southern Airlines is expected to raise HK$5 billion-HK$6 billion through a dual listing in Hong Kong and New York later in 1997, market sources said.

China National Aviation Corp (CNAC), the airline group controlled by China's Civil Aviation Administration which is expected to seek a listing in the third quarter, was likely to be a more eyecatching issue, analysts said.
They said strong parental backing and better earnings prospects made CNAC an attractive investment.
Last year CNAC bought a 36 percent controlling stake in Hong Kong Dragon Airlines from Swire Pacific Ltd, Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd, and CITIC Pacific Ltd.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's Ang said both China airlines and telecoms were for long-term investors.

"Fundamentally speaking, both the telecommunications and aviation sector are not that exciting," Ang said. "Enterprise demand for telecom and aviation services is temporarily saturated and that can slow their growth in the next two to five years.
"They will arouse interest from overseas investors who look for longer term growth in the industries," Ang said. "But they will not suit the appetite of local punters."
